full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division in Criminal Revision No. 54 of 1977 arising out of. G.R. No. 1308 of 1976 in the Court of Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Khulna, Sadar, Khulna. 

 4. The complainant stated in his complaint petition that the accused persons borrowed from time to time between the period 18.1.74 to 1 5.74 a sum of Tk. 25,500/- from the complainant for the purpose of their business. It is stated that the complainant brought pressure for repayment on 24.7.75 the accused No. 1 issued two cheques, one for Tk. 6,500/- and another for Tk. 19,000/- totaling Tk. 25,500/- towards the repayment but immediately sent a telegram from Chittagong stating that there is shortage of money in his account and cheque need not be presented. Subsequently it seems the parties have made up their affair and on the proposal of the complainant the accused persons agreed to work for him in his new venture in M/s Linker Enterprise. According to the complainant, he allowed them this facility to work for the purpose of realising his money and according to the defence it was the result of partnership arrangement and deed was executed on 26.4.76. The complainant stated in his petition that the accused petitioner No. 1 received a sum of Tk. 44,661/- on different dates for the purpose of the business and instead of depositing the amount in the account of Linkers Enterprise under the ownership of the complainant in Uttara Bank, Khulna, the accused No. 1 fraudulently beyond the knowledge of the complainant opened up another account in the name of Linkers Enterprise showing him as the owner of the firm with the Sonali Bank, Khulna being Account No. C.A. No. 5592 and dishonestly deposited the various amounts received on behalf of the Linkers Enterprise and thereby misappropriated the amount. Lastly the complainant stated that the accused No. 3 along with accused No. 1 withdrew Tk. 14756/- from the business fund on the plea of the marriage ceremony of the sister of accused No. 1 and on 4.3.76 accused Giasuddin in collusion with accused No. 3 took away Tk. 6,000/- from the business of the complainant and those amounts were taken without the consent of the complainant. The complainant stated that by their conduct and illegal activities the accused have committed an offence under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code. 

 6. The accused petitioners moved the High Court Division under section 561A Cr.P.C. for quashing the proceeding on the ground that the facts which have been set out do not constitute any criminal offence and therefore the criminal prosecution should be quashed. The learned Judges of the High Court Division discharged the rule by a cryptic order which is as follows: 

 It is regrettable that notwithstanding repeated reminders that when a litigant brings a litigation before the court he is entitled to a decision and adjudication of the dispute and such adjudication is to be performed in accordance with the laws of the country and the rules of procedure. Any deviation from such course is bound to affect administration of justice inasmuch as the whole system rests on public confidence and once the public confidence is shaken there ends the matter. 

 7. The allegations of the complainant which have been detailed above are mainly in four groups: (1) borrowing of Tk. 25,500/- on 18.1.74 to 1.5.74 and subsequent issuance of cheque towards repayment on 24 7.75 with a request not to present them before Bank, (2) complainant and the accused petitioner worked together in a common business enterprise namely M/s. Linkers Enterprise and while working together in this firm the accused persons misappropriated Tk. 44,66/-, (3) while working as such partner the accused persons withdrew Tk. 14,756/- from the business fund and another sum of Tk. 5,000/- for the purpose of marriage of sister of accused No. 1 without the consent of the complainant, (4) the complainant admitted that he entered into a partnership with the accused person on 26.4.76. 

 "In this petition for special leave a question has been raised, namely, when there was monetary transaction by way of borrowing and lending between the complainant respondent and the accused petitioner for a long time in the course of a partnership business any liability is a civil liability which can only be decided by a Civil Court and whether cognizance of such cases in the Criminal jurisdiction is an abuse of the process of the Court". 

 Since the High Court Division's judgment is only in two lines, no useful purpose will be served for looking for any guidance from such judgment. The learned Advocate had placed the entire complaint petition. The material question runs from page 44 to 49 of the paper book. His affidavit-in-opposition that was filed before the High Court Division in Criminal Revision is at pages 32 to 36. Gravamen of the charge against the accused have been mentioned above and the question is whether any criminal prosecution can be launched on such allegation. 

 12. The oldest case on the point is the Full Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Queen Vs. Okhoy Coomar. It was decided in 1874. In that decision it was said that where one partner is given authority by other partner to collect money or property of the firm then he is entrusted with a dominon over that property and if he dishonestly misappropriated it then be comes within this section. 

 13. This view of the Calcutta High Court since 1874 has been favoured with some force in the sub-continent. The Bombay High Court followed the case of Queen Vs. Okhoy Coomar in A.I.R. 1932 Bombay, 57 and the learned Chief Justice of Bombay expressed the opinion that when a partner is entrusted with dominion over the property and he dishonestly misappropriated it he comes within section 406 but the learned Chief Justice promptly issued a note of caution by adding as under: 

 "In these cases of charges against partners of criminal breach of trust, I think the Court ought to be very careful. In many cases it is impossible to say what the share of the accused may be, whether he is indebted to the firm or whether the firm is indebted to him and if the firm is indebted to him there may be no dishonest intent in his withdrawing money from the firm. If there is any doubt upon the matter, I think the accused must always have the benefit of the doubt. To some extent the question is one of degree." 

 The decision in the case of Okhoy Coomar held the field for about a century until 1951 when the question came before the Calcutta High Court again whether that case was correctly decided. In that case (Bhuban Mohan Das Vs. Surendra Mohan Das AIR 1951 Cal) the question was whether a partner can be charged under section 406 in respect of partnership property by another partner. It was a business of selling ghee, butter and stationary article. According to the complainant, the accused who was his partner pressed to him that the articles in the shop should be removed to the accused's house at Beniatala lane which was outside the affected area of communal riots. Complainant stated that he agreed whereupon the petitioner procured a taxi and loaded the articles and took them away. After some time the complainant asked for the articles but the accused stated that he had no knowledge of the articles at all. On this allegation a criminal prosecution was launched and the question was whether a charge under section 406 can be framed against a person who according to the complainant is a partner with him and is accused of the offence in respect of the property belonged to both of them as partner The second question was whether the decision in Queen Vs. Okhoy Coomar was correctly decided. 

 14. The reference first came before the Full Bench of 3 Judges but as the correctness of the earlier Full Bench case of Queen Vs. Okhoy Coomar had to be considered the Bench was constituted by 5 Judges and Chief Justice Harries presided over the Bench. Harries C.J. considered the question as to when a partner could be said to have acted in fiduciary capacity and the court relied on Paddock Vs Berge (1894, I Ch 349 that a partner who received payment of a debt due to the partnership firm did not hold the money in a fiduciary capacity and that no offence had been committed under the Debtors Act. The learned Chief Justice then reasoned that if the partner does not receive money in fiduciary capacity then he could not be charged with fraudulent breach of trust by reasons of his failing to account for that money. He considered that if the partner is holding property belonging to the partnership then he is holding it as one of the partners and entitled to hold it and it could not be said that he was holding it in a fiduciary capacity. Then it was observed: 

 16. As noticed in Bombay AI R 932(57). Mad AIR 1914 Mad 265, & Patna High Court AIR 1920 Patna 112 had followed the earlier Calcutta decision Now that the question bad been decided in the larger Bench of 5 Judges in Bhuhan Mohan Vs Surendra Das, A.I.R. 1951 Cal 69. The matter was in a flux for some time until it came before the Supreme Court of India in the case of Velji Raghwap Patel Vs. The State of Maharashtra reported in A.I.R. 1965 S.C. 1433 where the same question came before the Supreme Court and it was held that in case of partnership every partner has dominion over the partnership property by reason of the fact that he is a partner. It is a kind of dominion which every owner of property has over the property, But it is not dominion of kind which satisfies the requirement of section 405. The Supreme Court upheld the view of Harries, C.J. in A.I.R. 1951 Calcutta 69 and quoted with approval the passage from the Calcutta judgment. It was held further: 

 The Supreme Court, thus, had set the point at rest and the view that was expressed in the case of Okhoy Coomar was disapproved. 

 The question is whether there is any partnership is a question of fact. Next, whether a person who is concerned in the business is a mere creditor or his partner. In the case of ex parte Delhasse 1877-78 Volume VII Law Reports page 511 it was held that though an agreement is expressed to be an agreement for a loan to a partnership under sec. 1 of Bovill's Act, and contains a declaration that the lender shall not be a partner, he will nevertheless be a partner if the result of the agreement, fairly construed as a whole, independently of the reference to the Act and the declaration, is to give him the rights and impose on him the obligations of a partner". In Cox V. Hickman (1860) 8 SLC 268 the House of Lords settled the point that a participation in profits constitutes an invariable test of partnership is not one which can be maintained. Lord Cranworth, however, maintained the participation in profits is In general a sufficiently accurate test, and that the right of participation in profits affords cogent, often conclusive, evidence of a partner-ship. In Mollwo, March & Co. V. The Court of Wards, (1872) L.R. 4 P.C. 419 it was observed— 

 18. Keeping this principle in view there is no hesitation for saying that the complainant and the accused persons bad, as a matter of fact, entered into a partnership business even before the execution of the partnership deed on 26th April, 1976, Once it is held that it was a partnership business and the complainant and the accused persons were partners then on principle mentioned above namely, A.I.R. 1951 Calcutta which ultimately had been approved by the Supreme Court of India in A.I.R. 1965 (SC) at page 1433 such prosecution cannot be maintained. If the prosecution for criminal misappropriation cannot be maintained, the prosecution for cheating under section 420 cannot also be maintained. Analysing the section 415 Penal Code this court in the case of Akamuddin Ahmed Vs. The State. 27 DLR (AD) 175, 177) observed as under: 

 Having come to the conclusion that the prosecution under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code cannot be maintained, the question is whether the proceeding are liable to be quashed. In case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury Vs. Toe State. 28 DLR (AD) page 39 this Court considered the scope of section 561A Cr.P.C. and categories of cases for quashing before the trial. It was observed: 

 "Interference even it an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the court" 

 "the cases may also arise where the allegations in the first information report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged in such cases. No question of appreciating evidence arises, it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the criminal court to be issued against the accused person". 

 20. In the result therefore the appeal is allowed. Judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and the proceeding in G.R. Case No. 1308 of 1976 pending in the Court of Sub-Divisional Magistrate, 1st Class, Khulna is hereby quashed. 

 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother B. H. Chowdhury, J. and the views expressed by my learned brothel Masud, J. on the legal aspect of the matter While I am equally anxious to give relief to the accused-appellants, yet I feud no legal basis for making an order, at this stage quashing the proceeding simply on the ground that there is no proceeding against theta in the eye of law the matter is still at the stage of investigation by the police, and an order qua swing the proceeding will come in direct conflict with the decision of this Court in the case of Solicitor, Government of Bangladesh Vs. A.T. Mrida, 26 D.L.R. (SC) 17, besides running counter to the established principles governing quashment of criminal proceedings under section 561 at Cr.PC. As to the observation of this Court in the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury V. The State. 28 DLR (AD) 39 that 'Interference even at an initial stage may be justified". I find that 'Initial stage" as referred to, does not mean any stage prior to submission of the charge-sheet by the Police, bat it meant a state after submission of the charge-sheet. In the said case, the proceedings were sought to be quashed after Submission of the charge-sheet but ultimately the application for quashment was rejected and the appeal of the accused was dismissed. 

 22. In the instant case, a complaint was filed before the Magistrate on 10 June, 1976 bill the Magistrate forwarded it to the Police to treat it as First Information Report where-upon Khulna Police Case No. 90 was started on.21 June 1976. It appears that the police on receipt of the complaint treated it as F.I.R. and alerted investigation during, which they arrested the accused and produced them before the Court which ultimately released them on bail in the corresponding G.R Case No. 1308 of 1970 in usual course. But the accused within 7 months of the lodging of the First In-formation Report sought quashment of the proceedings by filing an application under section 561A of the Code of Crl. Procedure though the investigation was not yet completed. The application was liable to be summarily, rejected but a direction should have been given to expedite the investigation with-in a definite time. Instead, a Rule was issued, the application was registered as Crl. Revision No. 54 of 1977 on 31 January 1977 and all further proceedings, including investigation, were stayed till disposal of the Rule. The Rule was disposed of on 22 May 19,83, that is, after a period of over six years. It is unfortunate that a simple matter like this took such a lug time for disposal during which the entire machinery of investigation was put of gear. When the matter was disposed of, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erroneously held that the Magistrate issued processes against the accused under sections 406 and 420 of the Penal Code. Process is issued after cognizance is taken on a com-plaint, or on a police report or on the magistrate'; own knowledge In this case, the Magistrate did not yet take cognizance as no police report was yet submitted the matter remaining under investigation. The judgment of the High Court Division gave a wrong impression that cognizance was already taken and as such a criminal proceeding was pending against the appellants. The accused were arrested and produced before the Court during investigation. This has got nothing to do with the issuing of process. 

 23. As to the merit of the case, the First Information Report does not prima facie reveal commission of any criminal offence either of misappropriation or cheating excepting some adverse circumstances against the accused. That is why the Magistrate directed the investigation the result of which was required to be awaited. It cannot be said that the police deliberately prolonged the investigation, for within 7 month of the lodging of the First Information Report, the application for quashing the proceeding was filed and all further proceedings including the investigation were stayed. In the circumstances, the appropriate course would be to direct the police to complete the investigation and submit report within a short time, say 3 months, and to keep this appeal pending. As to the accused who are already on bail, they may not be required to appear before the Court till submission of the Police Report. This I think will give adequate remedy to the accused avoiding interference with the investigation by the Police. 

 27. Power under section 561A Cr.P.C. can be exercised from the purposes specified therein, namely (a) to give effect to any order under this Code; or (b) to prevent abuse of the process of any court or (3) otherwise to secure the ends of justice. 

 28. This Court has considered the scope of section 561A CrP.C. in two cases reported in 26 DLR (SC) 17 and 28 DLR (A.D) 39. The view taken in 26 DLR case is that statutory power of the police to investigate cognizable offence cannot be interfered with under section 561A and that section is not to be utilised to intercept or obstruct the ordinary course of procedure as laid down in the Code. 

 29. Proceeding before a Court starts when the Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on police report or on complaint. Before such cognizance, there is no proceeding that may be quashed under section 561A Cr.P.C. Process is issued only after taking of cognizance. In the 28 DLR case, this court considered as to when and under what circumstances jurisdiction under section 561A should be exercised and it was held that interference can be made even at the initial stage, when a mere perusal of the complaint would indicate that no criminal case stands against the accused. In that case there was however no discussion as to when a proceeding starts before a court. 

 30. In the instant case, no proceeding is pending before the Magistrate who referred the case to the Police for investigation under section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Police did not take up the case in pursuance of their statutory power to investigate a cognizable offence. The complaint was filed in 1976 and nothing is known about the result of the investigation. Each case is to be decided according to the facts and circumstances of that particular case. As the complaint petition does not disclose a prima facie criminal case against the appellant and as no proceeding is pending in any court the appropriate order in this appeal should be that the complaint be treated as dismissed and the appellant should be discharged from bail bond. 

 ORDER OF THE COURT 

 By the majority opinion the appeal is allowed and judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and the proceeding in G.R. Case No. 1308 of 1976 pending in the Court of Sub. Divisional Magistrate, 1st Class, Khulna is hereby quashed.
